title: Compassion close
hook: compassion can grow, with practice and time

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was ten minutes of compassion: you, someone dear, someone neutral, someone hard, then everyone. Your line was may you be well.

A farmer in the state of Song is worried: his grain is coming up too slowly. So he goes out and, one by one, tugs every young stalk upward a little, to help it along. He comes home worn out and announces he's been helping the crop grow. His son runs out to look. Every plant has withered. The philosopher Mencius tells this story, and it fits the end of a stretch about something that grows. Today the section on compassion closes, by asking how it grows.
screen: `A FARMER IN SONG.` → `TUGGING EVERY STALK.` → `THE WHOLE FIELD WITHERED.`

segments.voice: First, the sprout. Mencius, in the book that carries his name, says anyone who suddenly saw a child about to fall into a well would feel alarm and distress, not for a reward or a reputation, simply because. In James Legge's translation: "The feeling of commiseration is the principle of benevolence." He calls feelings like this beginnings, small shoots in every person that can grow or wither. Second, the farmer. A sprout can be harmed two ways: by neglect, never weeding, or by yanking on it to hurry it. On his telling, goodness grows the way grain grows: tended, daily, without force. Third, the evidence, at its own scale. The research this path walked through points the same way. Short programs measured gains in compassion. Weeks of loving-kindness moved one measure of bias. Real changes, modest in size, while some headlines claimed far more, about the vagus nerve and the love hormone. It grows like grain, not like a magic bean. Fourth, the look back, in this section's lines: warmth, not drowning. Care for carers. Trainable. Wider. The seat. Not in a hurry. Be the one. For someone else. It spreads. Softer inside. Modest claims. Not so simple. Pass it on. Their side. The circle widens. Fierce and kind. Care heals. Me too. May you be well. A whole field of sprouts, none of them tugged.
screen: `A CHILD AT THE EDGE OF A WELL.` · `DON'T NEGLECT IT, DON'T TUG IT.` · `GRAIN, NOT A MAGIC BEAN.` · `A WHOLE FIELD OF SPROUTS.` · then, large: `IT GROWS.`

segments.voice: Walk back over the last few weeks and look for one change the size of a sprout: a moment you wished someone well instead of drowning in their trouble, a seat you gave up, a kinder sentence to yourself after a mistake. Don't tug on it to make it bigger than it was. If nothing comes, that's an honest answer too; it just means keep weeding.
Compassion close. The end of this section: compassion as a sprout, grown by tending, slowly, with practice and time. Today's word.
Your line: it grows. Tended, slowly, without force, the way grain grows. And with that, the section closes.

howItsDone: In the Confucian tradition, Mencius's "four beginnings" are taught as sprouts of goodness that grow through steady cultivation; some contemplative programs also ask people to keep a simple record of small changes over time.

fork.setup: in Mencius's story, the farmer of Song thinks his grain is coming up too slowly. what does he do?
options: tug every stalk upward a little, to help it along.
stop weeding, since nothing seems to work.
fork.reveal: he tugs every stalk, comes home proud, and the whole field withers. Mencius warns against both his mistake and its opposite, neglect.

original.note: Classical Chinese, from the Mencius: the heart of commiseration, one of his four beginnings.

chat.says: If compassion can be trained, why not push hard and get there fast?
options: Mencius says tugging a sprout kills it; goodness grows like grain, tended daily, without force.
Pushing hard is the point; the studies show big changes come fast if you really try.
It can't really grow; you're either born caring or you aren't, so training won't help.
chat.meaning: In Mencius's story, the farmer who tugged his grain killed it. Compassion grows by steady tending, and the research found real but modest changes.

Mencius.meaning: a Confucian philosopher who taught that goodness grows like a sprout

Song.meaning: an ancient Chinese state, home of the farmer in the story

commiseration.meaning: feeling sorrow with someone who suffers

benevolence.meaning: goodwill: the wish and habit of doing good

vagus nerve.meaning: a long nerve linking the brain with the heart and gut

sources.quoted: The feeling of commiseration is the principle of benevolence

notes: Confirm the Legge wording of Mencius 2A:6: 'The feeling of commiseration is the principle of benevolence.' (Legge's Chinese Classics vol. 2.)

The child-at-the-well passage (2A:6) is paraphrased. Legge spells the state 'Sung'; the voice uses the pinyin 'Song'. The tugged-grain story is from 2A:2 and is paraphrased, including Mencius's two errors (neglect, not weeding; forcing, pulling up).
